747SP Sets Around-the-World Record
By Rosalind K. Ellingsworth
New York-Pan American World Airways Boeing 747SP record-setting flight around
the world was a demonstration of the long-range capability, comfort and convenience
of current air transport technology.
The flight of Pan American's second-
delivered 747SP, which was called Clip-
per Liberty Bell, was a scheduled extra
section revenue flight. More than that, it
was a public relations tactic thought up
by a Pan American pilot that caught the
imagination of at least 71 persons, who
paid either $2,927 for a first-class ticket or
$1,865 for a coach ticket.
The flight was generally planned
around the longest segment of more than
8,000 mi., New York-New Delhi. Fuel re-
quirements and weight restrictions for
that leg limited passenger capacity to no
more than 130 persons.
At one point during the planning for
the flight, 132 persons were on the pas-
senger list, but several revenue passengers
canceled as departure time neared. At
takeoff, there were 20 paying first-class
passengers and 51 coach passengers on
board.
Departure from the gate at John F.
Kennedy International in New York was
5:23 p.m. EDT May 1, or 2123 Green-
wich Mean Time. Return to the gate,
while planned for 1 p.m. EDT May 3,
was actually at 3:50 p.m. May 3, or 1950
GMT. Total time from gate to gate was
46 hr. 18 min. 40 sec.
The record, however, was established
on a takeoff to touchdown time of 46 hr.
50 sec. Total air time for the flight was 39
hr. 25 min. 53 sec., or 4 min. 7 sec. under
the original flight plan.
The record time, which was verified by
an official from the National Aeronautics
Assn., the U.S. representative of the Fed-
eration Aeronautique Internationale,
broke the standing record of 62 hr. 27
min. 35 sec.
The old record had been set in Novem-
ber, 1965, by a Boeing 707-320C. The
new 46-hr. 50-sec. record time includes
transit times at New Delhi and Tokyo.
Pan American had planned a new
record time of 43 hr. 30 min., but a labor
dispute with airport ground workers in
Tokyo increased the transit time there by
2 hr. 1 min. The Tokyo dispute was no
surprise to Pan American officials, who
had known for about two weeks prior to
the flight that ground workers at Haneda
International had been delaying depar-
tures for a number of airlines.
Airline officials decided to take the risk
of a possible delay in Tokyo because they
had advertised the record-breaking flight
with a stop in that city and wanted to ad-
here to their preflight planning.
A 2-hr. transit time had been planned
for Tokyo and passengers were re-
boarded, after ceremonies in the terminal
building, to comply with that time sched-
ule. Once on board, however, passengers
were informed by Capt. Walter H. Mulli-
kin, Pan American's vice president and
chief pilot and head of the 15-man cock-
pit crew for the record flight, that ground
workers had parked equipment behind
the 747SP's wings and at least one ground
worker was sitting on a high stool under
the belly of the aircraft.
Rush S. Clark, Pan American manag-
ing director in Tokyo, negotiated with
members of the Japanese Airport Em-
ployes' Union, a national union, to obtain
release of the aircraft. Calculations were
quickly made on board and constantly
updated to determine the final possible
minute the aircraft would have to depart
to establish the sought-for 43-hr. 30-min.
block-to-block time.
There was never much of a risk to like-
lihood of establishing a new world record
for a transport category aircraft because
of the large difference between the stand-
ing record of more than 62hr. and the
current aircraft capabilities.
During negotiations with the union, the
decision was made to take on 12,000 lb.
of fuel in order to fly the last segment at
higher-than-planned speeds to adhere to
the advertised promise of circling the
globe in 39.5 hr.
Other than the Tokyo incident, which
for the passengers provided a bit of diver-
sionary excitement and prompted talk of
jumping ship for a Japanese hot bath, the
record-setting flight went according to
schedule.
The New York-New Delhi segment of
8,088 mi. was completed in 13 hr. 57 min.
gate-to-gate. Average air speed on the
first segment was 598.146 mph. Total de-
parture weight from New York was
660,700 Ib., 330,700 Ib. of that in fuel.
Fuel consumed during the segment to-
taled 41,099 gal., or 276,600 lb. Enough
fuel remained (54,100 lb.) that the flight
could have gone on to Bangkok and still
had required reserves: Highest cruise alti-
tude of 45,000 ft. reached during the total
flight was on the New York-New Delhi
segment.
Arrival at the gate in New Delhi was at
1120 GMT May 2, and departure was at
Aviation Week & Space Technology, May 17, 1976
